question: Which body system does your skin belong to?
explanation: You got it! The skin is part of the integumentary system, which also includes your hair, nails, and glands that keep your body safe. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is the skin considered our body's primary shield?

options.A: It sits right between our internal organs and the outside world.
options.B: It produces all our red blood cells.
options.C: It pumps nutrients directly into underlying muscles.
options.D: It filters waste straight out of our bloodstream.

explanation: Spot on! Because skin covers our entire outside, it acts as our very first line of defense against everyday hazards. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h1)

question: What tough protein gives the outer layer of our skin its strength?
explanation: Great job! Keratin is a tough, fibrous protein that makes our outer skin cells strong and durable. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h2)

question: If a patient scrapes the surface of their skin without a deep cut, which layer took the hit?
explanation: Correct! The stratum corneum is the very top layer of the epidermis, meaning it handles all the daily friction and minor scrapes. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the normal pH range of the skin's protective acid mantle?
explanation: Well done! A slightly acidic pH between 4.5 and 5.5 makes it hard for harmful bacteria and fungi to grow on us. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h3)

question: How do sebum (skin oil) and sweat team up to protect your body?

options.A: They combine to form an acid mantle that stops germs from growing.
options.B: They cool down internal organs by freezing surface blood vessels.
options.C: They create a thick physical padding against heavy bumps.
options.D: They digest food particles absorbed through the skin.

explanation: Exactly! Sebum and sweat mix on the skin to create the acid mantle, turning the skin into a tough environment for germs. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the main job of Langerhans cells in the skin?

options.A: Sensing cold temperatures and gentle touches
options.B: Producing oily sebum to keep the skin soft and waterproof
options.C: Making the dark pigment that shields against sunlight
options.D: Catching and processing foreign invaders for the immune system

explanation: You got it! Langerhans cells are like security guards in the skin—they catch microbes and run to the lymph nodes to sound the alarm. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h4)

question: Where in the skin are Langerhans cells mostly found?
explanation: Spot on! They hang out right in the epidermis so they can easily catch any germs trying to sneak in from the outside. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which specialized skin cells make the pigment melanin?
explanation: Correct! Melanocytes are the clever cells in our lower epidermis that produce melanin. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h5)

question: How does melanin protect our skin cells from ultraviolet (UV) rays?

options.A: It absorbs and scatters UV rays before they damage cell DNA.
options.B: It freezes the skin surface to block hot sunlight.
options.C: It neutralizes sweat acids to stop sunburns.
options.D: It thickens the outer skin into a hard shell.

explanation: Well done! Melanin acts as your body's built-in umbrella, soaking up and scattering harmful UV rays away from your cell nuclei. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h5)

question: What do blood vessels in the skin do when your body needs to release extra heat?
explanation: Spot on! When they widen (dilate), warm blood moves closer to the skin surface so excess body heat can escape into the air. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h6)

question: How does the skin keep your body from drying out?

options.A: Skin lipids form a watertight seal that stops fluid from evaporating.
options.B: Sweat glands constantly pump moisture backward into the blood.
options.C: Melanin absorbs water vapor right out of the air.
options.D: Keratin fibers store up large amounts of liquid fat.

explanation: You got it! The natural oils (lipids) between our skin cells trap moisture inside, keeping us nicely hydrated. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h6)

question: A patient has severe burns across a large part of their body. What is the nurse's biggest immediate worry?

options.B: Sudden thickening of the outer skin layer
options.D: Fluid loss and risk of infection

explanation: Spot on, nurse! When skin is badly damaged, it can't hold body fluids in or keep germs out, making dehydration and infection major emergencies. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why does a cut or break in the skin raise a patient's risk of getting sick?

options.A: Harmful germs can slip straight into the body without any barrier.
options.B: Langerhans cells stop working during healing.
options.C: Skin oil production increases so much that it traps bacteria.
options.D: The skin stops sweating, causing internal organs to overheat.

explanation: Great job! A whole skin barrier blocks germs effortlessly; once that barrier breaks, microbes have an open doorway into deeper tissues. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h7)
